summary: Specifies a relay element for PANA, a protocol that carries network access authentication. The relay lets a client and an authentication agent exchange PANA messages even when ordinary IP routing cannot connect them directly.

eli5.summary: When you want to talk to someone but cannot reach them directly, a friend can pass notes between you. A PANA relay does this for messages about logging into a network.

questions: pana client cannot reach authentication agent
what is a pana relay element
what is the pana udp port
how does pana work across multiple hops
subtitle: A relay node that lets PANA clients and authentication agents talk when normal IP routing cannot connect them.

tldr.problem: PANA carries network access authentication over UDP, but a joining device may only be able to use a link-local address and so cannot reach a PANA Authentication Agent that is several IP hops away.
tldr.mechanism: A PANA Relay Element wraps each PANA message in a PANA-Relay message with a Relayed-Message AVP and a PaC-Information AVP, and forwards it to the agent, which replies the same way.
tldr.outcome: The relay needs no per-client state. Securing the relay-to-agent link is optional but IPsec is the recommended mechanism.

today: RFC 6345 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2011. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on the PANA base protocol in RFC 5191.

sections.title: The Reachability Problem
sections.content:
PANA (RFC 5191) is a UDP-based protocol that performs Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) authentication between a PANA Client (PaC) and a PANA Authentication Agent (PAA). RFC 6345 adds PANA Relay Element (PRE) functionality for cases where the PaC and PAA cannot reach each other by regular IP routing.

The motivating example is ZigBee IP over 6LoWPAN (RFC 4944). A joining node can only use a link-local IPv6 address to talk to its parent node before authentication. The PAA typically sits in a 6LoWPAN Border Router, often several IP hops away. The PRE runs on the parent node and relays PANA messages in between.
sections.eli5: A new device can only whisper to its neighbor, but the one who decides who may join is far away. The neighbor passes the messages along.

sections.title: How Relaying Works
sections.content:
A PRE sits between a PaC and a PAA. From the PaC's view, the PRE appears to be the PAA, and the PaC finds it by the normal PAA discovery of RFC 5192. PREs are assumed to be configured with the PAA addresses; dynamic PAA discovery for PREs is out of scope. A PAA can work with many PREs, and a PRE can know several PAAs but picks one for a given PaC.

When the PRE receives a PANA message from the PaC, it builds a PANA-Relay (PRY) message holding the whole message in a Relayed-Message AVP and the PaC's IP address and UDP port in a PaC-Information AVP, and sends it to the PAA. The PAA unwraps it and processes the message as in RFC 5191, with three exceptions: it uses the PaC address and port together with the PRE's source address and port to tell PaCs apart, it stores the PaC address and port in the session attribute, and it stores the PRE address and port in a new session attribute. A session with a non-null value there is a relayed PANA session.

To reply, the PAA sends a PRY message to the stored PRE address and port. The PRE unwraps it and sends the inner message to the PaC's address, with source UDP port 716 (the PANA port) and destination port taken from the PaC-Information AVP.

Session Identifier and Sequence Number of any PRY message are zero, and PRY messages are never retransmitted. If the PaC or PAA retransmits the inner message, a new PRY carrying it is sent. A PAA that supports this specification MUST be able to process PRY messages for PaC-initiated sessions. At most one PRE between PaC and PAA is assumed.
sections.eli5: The helper puts each note in an envelope marked with who wrote it, sends it on, and later takes the answer out of its envelope and hands it to the right person. The helper does not need to remember anyone.

sections.title: The PANA-Relay Message and AVPs
sections.content:
The PANA-Relay message (PRY) goes from PRE to PAA or from PAA to PRE. It contains one PaC-Information AVP and one Relayed-Message AVP, and SHOULD NOT carry other AVPs. Its header uses message type 5, and the Session Identifier and Sequence Number MUST be zero. A PRY message MUST NOT be retransmitted.

In a PAA-originated PRY, the PaC-Information content MUST be copied from the session attribute holding the PaC's address and port.

  • PaC-Information (AVP Code 10): an OctetString with the IP address (4 octets for IPv4, 16 for IPv6) followed by a 2-octet UDP port, in network byte order.
  • Relayed-Message (AVP Code 11): an OctetString with the relayed PANA message, excluding the UDP and IP headers.
sections.eli5: The envelope has two parts: a label with the sender's address and door number, and the original note inside. Nothing else belongs in it.

sections.title: An Example Exchange
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows a PaC, a PRE and a PAA. The PaC sends a PANA-Client-Initiation (PCI) to the PRE. The PRE forwards it in a PRY to the PAA on port 716. The PAA answers with a PRY wrapping a PANA-Auth-Request (PAR), and the PRE hands the PAR to the PaC. The PaC replies with a PANA-Auth-Answer (PAN), which is relayed the same way, and the pattern repeats.

The PRE may use the same IP address towards the PaC and the PAA, or two different ones. It uses its own UDP port towards the PAA.
sections.eli5: The newcomer says hello, the helper carries it up, and the answer comes back down the same path, over and over until the check is done.

sections.title: Securing the Relay Path
sections.content:
Security between PRE and PAA is OPTIONAL because PANA is designed for untrusted networks. If a cryptographic mechanism is supported, it SHOULD be IPsec. Where a device cannot support IPsec, alternatives such as DTLS (RFC 4347) or link-layer security may be used. The IPsec profile uses selectors based on configured PRE and PAA address pairs on port 716, transport mode with ESP (NULL encryption is acceptable since PANA data is not generally confidential), and IKE with preshared secrets, which SHOULD be supported. IKE with public keys MAY be supported. Manually keyed setups do not protect against replayed messages.

The Security Considerations section notes that a PRE can delay, drop, spoof or modify messages, much like an on-path bridge or router, and that EAP and PANA are designed to work over insecure links. These threats cannot be used to gain unauthorized network access or compromise keys, but denial of service is still possible. A rogue PRE could spoof messages for a victim PaC and receive the PAA's response from anywhere, yet cannot complete full authentication without the PaC's credentials. Because PREs keep no per-PaC state, they resist resource-exhaustion attacks. The residual risks are to be mitigated with physical or cryptographic security and access control lists around the PREs and PAAs.
sections.eli5: The helper could be tricked or could be a bad helper, but without the secret password it still cannot get a stranger into the network. Locking the hallway between helper and office makes it even safer.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: Following the PANA IANA rules of RFC 5872, one message type and two AVP codes were assigned: message type 5 for PANA-Relay (PRY) with the Request bit cleared, AVP Code 10 for PaC-Information and AVP Code 11 for Relayed-Message.
sections.eli5: Three numbers were officially reserved so that nobody else uses them for something different: one for the envelope and two for its parts.
